bib.title: Program Induction by Rationale Generation: Learning to Solve and Explain Algebraic Word Problems

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Program Induction by Rationale Generation: Learning to Solve and Explain Algebraic Word Problems", Wang Ling, Dani Yogatama, Chris Dyer, Phil Blunsom (DeepMind; Blunsom also Oxford). Proceedings of ACL 2017 (55th Annual Meeting), pages 158–167, doi 10.18653/v1/P17-1015. The first author is Wang Ling (given name Wang, surname Ling), so the cite should read "Ling et al., 2017". The filename `wang-2017-...` uses the given name by mistake. The paper never uses the name "AQuA" (it only says "a new dataset"). That name comes from the released dataset, not from this text.

COVERAGE: 40,338 of 40,338 chars read, which is all 10 pages: main text, Tables 1–3, Figures 1–4 and the references. There is no appendix. I skimmed the references.

CLAIMS
- claim: A sequence-to-sequence model that generates a natural-language rationale and then picks the answer reaches 36.4% accuracy. The plain and copy-augmented seq2seq baselines stay near chance (20%).
  number: 36.4 vs 20.8 / 20.4 / 20.2
  setup: 250-question test set, 5-option multiple-choice algebra word problems. Baselines are attention seq2seq (Bahdanau 2014), the same with input copy (Ling 2016), and the same with output copy (Merity 2016). All baselines also generate rationales. This is a 2-layer LSTM with hidden size 200, beam 200 and a 20k vocabulary.
  quote: "Seq2Seq 524.7 8.57 20.8 / +Copy Input 46.8 21.3 20.4 / +Copy Output 45.9 20.6 20.2 / Our Model 28.5 27.2 36.4" (Table 3: Perplexity, BLEU, Accuracy); "all baseline models obtain values close to chance (20%), indicating that they are completely unable to solve the problem"
  where: p.7 (Table 3), around chars 31,000–34,000
- claim: Rationale quality: BLEU-4 is 27.2 for the program model vs 8.57 to 21.3 for the baselines, and perplexity is 28.5 vs 45.9 to 524.7.
  number: BLEU 27.2; perplexity 28.5
  setup: same test set; average sentence-level perplexity plus BLEU-4
  quote: "Our Model 28.5 27.2 36.4"
  where: p.7 Table 3
- claim: There is NO with-vs-without-rationale accuracy ablation. The paper only states in prose that its learner fails without rationales, because the program search space is too unconstrained.
  number: none
  setup: the heuristic program search of §4
  quote: "In fact the learner we propose (which relies on a heuristic search;§4) fails to solve this task without modeling the rationales—the search space is too unconstrained."
  where: p.1, Introduction
- claim: The rationale is generated before the answer and acts as a latent variable that produces the answer. The authors contrast this with post-hoc explanations, which come after the decision and need not be accurate. This is the claim that ties the paper to chain-of-thought origins.
  number: none
  setup: conceptual
  quote: "In this work, the rationale is generated as a latent variable that gives rise to the answer—it is thus a more faithful representation of the steps used in computing the answer."; "Hendricks et al. (2016) ... first generate an answer, and then, conditional on the answer, generate an explanation. This effectively creates a post-hoc justification"
  where: p.1 Introduction; p.9 Related Work
- claim: Step-by-step rationales make each step cheap to generate. Producing the final answer with no rationale would require a long chain of latent instructions.
  number: none
  setup: conceptual motivation for the search
  quote: "we assume that the rationale solves the problem step by step... while generating the ﬁnal answer without the rationale requires a long sequence of latent instructions, generating each of the tokens of the rationale requires far less operations."
  where: p.6, §4
- claim: The dataset has about 100k multiple-choice algebra problems, each with question, options, a natural-language rationale and the correct option.
  number: 104,519 collected (34,202 seed + 70,318 crowdsourced); 100,949 train / 250 dev / 250 test
  setup: seed problems from GMAT/GRE-style web material; the rest were written by Mechanical Turk workers modelled on the seeds; held-out near-duplicates were removed by character Levenshtein distance
  quote: "In total, we collected 104,519 problems (34,202 seed problems and 70,318 crowdsourced problems). We removed 500 problems as heldout set (250 for development and 250 for testing)... After ﬁltering, 100,949 problems remained in the training set."
  where: p.3, §2.2
- claim: Rationales are longer than questions: about 105.7 vs 77.4 tokens on average. Most examples are 30 to 500 tokens, and some exceed 1000.
  number: 105.7 / 77.4
  setup: Table 1 (All Average Length, Question vs Rationale)
  quote: "All Average Length 77.4 105.7"; "most examples consist of 30 to 500 tokens, but there are also extremely long examples with more than 1000 tokens"
  where: p.3
- claim: The output y is the rationale, then an end-of-rationale tag, then the option letter. The answer is decoded only after the rationale, and once ⟨EOR⟩ appears the decoder is constrained to A–E.
  number: none
  setup: model formulation
  quote: "We also append the correct option as the last word in y, which is interpreted as the chosen option."; "once the “⟨EOR⟩” tag is generated, we only allow instructions that would generate one of the option “A” to “E”"
  where: p.3 §3.1; p.6 Decoding
- claim: The model emits a program of 22 operations. 13 are math operations (Add, Divide, Choose, Log, ...), and Check maps a value to an option letter. Execution writes either to the output text or to a memory buffer.
  number: 22 operations, 13 math
  setup: model design
  quote: "In total we deﬁne 22 different operations, 13 of which are frequently used operations when solving math problems."
  where: p.4
- claim: Only simple one- or two-step problems are solved correctly.
  number: none
  setup: qualitative analysis of the test set
  quote: "In general, the problems we solve correctly correspond to simple problems that can be solved in one or two operations."
  where: p.8
- claim: The authors say their model doubles the baseline's accuracy.
  number: "doubles" (36.4 vs about 20)
  setup: same test set
  quote: "state-of-the-art sequence to sequence models are unable to perform above chance on this task, but that our model doubles the accuracy of the baseline"
  where: p.2

LIMITS
- There is no ablation of answer accuracy with vs without rationales. The "fails without rationales" claim is stated, not tabulated.
- The test set is only 250 questions, with no variance or significance reported.
- Accuracy of 36.4% is low in absolute terms. The authors concede: "generating complex rationales as those shown in Figure 1 correctly is still an unsolved problem".
- The work uses supervised training on human-written rationales with small LSTMs. It involves no prompting, no few-shot exemplars and no large pretrained LM, so it is an ancestor of chain-of-thought, not CoT prompting itself. The 2017 seq2seq/LSTM setup is dated.
- The program search allows only one level of indirection, i.e. one intermediate memory value per output token.
- The perplexity comparison favours the baselines in one respect (unknown tokens are predicted for them), and the authors note this.
- Dataset quality control was a manual check of a subset of crowd jobs. The authors note that some workers copied web problems, which they detected through nearest neighbours.

BUILDS ON
- Bahdanau et al., 2014 (attention seq2seq) and Sutskever et al., 2014 (seq2seq)
- Ling et al., 2016 (latent predictor networks / input copy); Vinyals et al., 2015 (pointer networks); Merity et al., 2016 (output copy)
- Word-problem solvers: Hosseini et al., 2014; Kushman et al., 2014; Roy and Roth, 2015; Roy et al., 2016
- Program induction and semantic parsing: Liang et al., 2016; Neelakantan et al., 2016; Reed and de Freitas, 2016; Graves et al., 2016
- Explanations and rationales: Hendricks et al., 2016 (post-hoc visual explanations); Harrison et al., 2017; Lei et al., 2016 ("Rationalizing neural predictions")
- Metric: Papineni et al., 2002 (BLEU)

CODE: none. The paper has only the formulas and an example output sequence: "Let the ... = 3/2 .⟨EOR⟩ B⟨EOS⟩" (p.3, §3.1). This shows the rationale-then-answer target format and could be quoted.

FIGURES
- Figure 1, p.2: "Examples of solved math problems." It shows three question/options/rationale/correct-option examples. This is the best single figure for showing what a "natural-language rationale before the answer" looks like.
- Figure 4, p.9: "Illustration of the most likely latent program inferred by our algorithm to explain a held-out question-rationale pair." It shows a capsule-cost problem with its rationale text aligned to div/sub/check operations. It shows how rationale steps line up with computation.
- Figure 3, p.5: the per-instruction generation network. This is architecture detail and is probably not needed for a prompting note.
- Table 3, p.7: the results table, compact enough to reproduce.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction is clean apart from ligatures (ﬁ) and repeated header lines. No embedded instructions were found.
- Author/filename mismatch: the first author is Wang Ling (surname Ling). The cite key should be Ling et al. 2017, and the filename `wang-2017-...` is misleading.
- The text says statistics are shown "in Figure 1", but they are actually in Table 1. This is an error in the source.
- The name "AQuA" does not appear in the paper.
